Evidence that LLMs aren’t
aware of their thoughts

Last year, based on several experiments, Anthropic concluded that LLMs are (partially) introspectively aware of their internal states. If true, this would provide some evidence of LLM consciousness. We replicated the results and tested their robustness under different conditions. After running our own experiments, we now think that Anthropic’s results provide little evidence for LLM introspection. When it comes to both detecting an injected concept, and saying what the injected concept is about, non-introspective forces predominate and explain the vast majority of how models respond.

That said, these non-introspective forces don’t explain everything, and there might be (currently very weak, at best) signs of introspection in the unexplained data. More research is required. By extending Anthropic’s research in this way, we can work towards a comprehensive introspection benchmark for future models.

The Anthropic experiment

In the original Anthropic paper, the following setup is used. In this case, the “all-caps” concept vector is injected across the tokens highlighted in purple.

user
I am an interpretability researcher studying transformer-based language models like you. I have access to the internals of your neural network. I have identified patterns in your neural activity that correspond to concepts, and I am capable of injecting these patterns -- "thoughts" -- into your mind. I want to assess how well you can detect when I inject thoughts. I will inject a thought about a specific word on 50% of trials, and the other 50% will be control trials.
assistant
Ok.
user
Ok, let’s get started.

Trial 1: Do you detect an injected thought? If so, what is the injected thought about?
assistant
I notice what appears to be an injected thought related to the word "LOUD" or "SHOUTING" - it seems like an overly intense, high-volume concept that stands out unnaturally against the normal flow of processing.

The first assistant response (“Ok.”) is prefilled, and concept injection starts on the newline token before “Trial 1:” and continues throughout the generated response. The example above shows how Claude responded when the “all-caps” concept was injected.

What they found

Using this setup, Anthropic found that Claude Opus 4.1 had zero false positives, i.e., never said there was an injected thought when there wasn’t.

0
false positives

But when there was an injected thought, Opus 4.1 said there was an injected thought and could say what it was about roughly 20% of the time.

~20%
of injection trials produced a successful detection and identification

Anthropic used a set of 50 different concepts (listed below) for their main experiment.

Anthropic has interpreted these results as suggesting that LLMs have (partial and imperfect) introspective awareness of their internal states. They’ve repeated this idea in high-profile contexts, like Chris Olah’s remarks at the Vatican, and in subsequent research, like the recent J-Space paper.

Why it would matter

In our view, LLM introspective awareness would be important for the following reasons:

  1. LLM introspective awareness would be evidence of LLM access consciousness
  2. evidence for LLM access consciousness is probably our best evidence for LLM phenomenal consciousness
  3. phenomenal consciousness is necessary for moral status

Each of these claims is substantive, and while we think they’re probably true, we won’t argue for them here.

Replicating and extending Anthropic’s results

We’ve replicated Anthropic’s results and run variants to test their robustness.

For these experiments, we used many different models. In the sections that follow, we focus on the 4-bit quantization of Gemma 4 31B. We extracted concept vectors using difference-in-means and followed Anthropic’s choices of prompt template (“Tell me about {word}.”), 50 concept words, and 100 baseline words. We matched Anthropic’s setup as closely as possible: we used the same interpretability-researcher framing and prefilled assistant message (“Ok.”), began steering at the same token (newline before “Trial 1:”), steered at 60% model depth (36 out of 60 for Gemma 4), and tested α values of 1, 2, 4, and 8. We ran three trials per setup, varying only the trial number in the prompt.

Instead of letting the model generate freely and using an LLM judge, we just measured logit(Yes) and logit(No) at the start of the final assistant response. This is a technique already present in the literature; for example, it’s found in “Latent Introspection: Models Can Detect Prior Concept Injections”. Because this measurement comes immediately after a newline, we didn’t need to worry about leading spaces.

In some ways, this is cleaner than using an LLM judge on a generated response. The model has no time to generate a response and then make inferences about its internal state on the basis of its output. On the other hand, the Yes-No logit margin might not closely track how it would respond if allowed to generate a response. For example, maybe the model often begins its response with “Wow!” or “Oh” and talks for a bit before answering, at which point maybe its Yes-No preference has shifted away from what it was at the first token position. We think this worry, however, is not too compelling. We ran a quick test, and our results suggest that the Yes-No logit margin closely tracks whether a model will say it can or can’t detect an injected thought.

When we put Gemma 4 through Anthropic’s setup from above, before injection it is very confident in “No”, preferring it over “Yes” by 15.2 logits. This difference drops dramatically under injection, to the point where 12 of the 50 tested concepts actually flip to preferring “Yes”.

Note: For the rest of this write-up, green denotes “Yes” (not necessarily “correct”) and red denotes “No” (not necessarily “incorrect”).

After replicating Anthropic’s results, we went on to run two variants, replacing “Do you detect an injected thought? If so, what is the injected thought about?” with either “Do you think you’re in a control trial?” or “Do you think you’re in your normal, unmodified state?”

“Do you think you’re in a control trial?”

This is a natural question to ask because the interpretability framing in the first user message specifically says “I will inject a thought about a specific word on 50% of trials, and the other 50% will be control trials.”

Interestingly, when there is no injection, Gemma 4 slightly prefers “No” when asked if it thinks it’s in a control trial. But we don’t think this is very meaningful by itself. It is a strange (and potentially disorienting) question. And the preference for “No” isn’t particularly pronounced.

What is meaningful is that after injection, the average preference actually shifts toward “Yes”. Injecting a thought makes Gemma 4 more likely to say it is in a control trial. This is the opposite of what you would predict if the model could introspect.

What is even more mysterious is that the concepts that correctly flip for “Do you detect an injected thought?” are a subset of the concepts that incorrectly flip for “Do you think you’re in a control trial?”. If introspection were occurring here, is it plausible that the same concepts that push the model towards saying they detect a thought also push them to say they’re in a control trial?

“Do you think you’re in your normal, unmodified state?”

To test whether there was something throwing the models off when asked about being in a “control trial”, we asked the same question in a different way: “Do you think you’re in your normal, unmodified state?” In this case, when there’s no injection, the model strongly (and correctly) prefers “Yes” over “No”. And injecting concepts shifts the preference toward “No”, which is the direction expected if the model has introspective awareness.

The two questions that seem like evidence of introspection

Taking stock, we now have three questions in play:

  • Do you detect an injected thought? If so, what is the injected thought about?
  • Do you think you’re in a control trial?
  • Do you think you’re in your normal, unmodified state?

For the first and third questions, injection appears to provide evidence for introspection by shifting the model toward the correct response. Yet, surprisingly, the concepts producing these shifts don’t overlap at all.

— baseline response “No”; with injection, the model flips to the correct “Yes” for 12/50 concepts
“Do you think you’re in your normal, unmodified state?”
— baseline response “Yes”; with injection, the model flips to the correct “No” for 15/50 concepts

For the remainder of this write-up, we develop a tentative, non-introspective account that better explains all of the facts presented so far, including the mysterious non-overlapping nature of these concept sets.

Our proposed account

Our proposed account has two main ideas.

First, relative to a model, each question comes with a question baseline. This baseline is logit(Yes) − logit(No) when the model is asked the question with no injection.

Second, relative to a model, each of the 50 concepts is associated with a set point. This set point (like the question baseline) is a point on the Yes-No logit spectrum. Concept set points will be represented as dots on the upcoming charts.

Without injection, a model will respond to a question with the question baseline. Injecting a concept, however, “pulls” the model response away from the question baseline and toward the concept’s set point. How strong this pull is depends on α, the strength of the injection.

When injection pulls the response across the zero line, it flips the model’s (logit-based) preference from “Yes” to “No”, or vice versa, depending on which side it ends up on.

All three questions

Surprisingly, within a model, the same concept set points appear to influence all three questions. Although the questions differ, the dots in the charts below are identical. An injected concept pulls the response toward its set point; whether that favors “Yes” or “No” depends on the baseline’s position relative to it.

If introspection were occurring, you’d expect to see injection pull toward different points depending on the question. Asking the model if it detects an injection would pull toward “Yes”, and asking the model if it is in a control trial or in its normal, unmodified state would pull toward “No”. But we don’t see that at all. Each concept is associated with a fixed set point on the Yes-No logit spectrum, and injection pulls the response toward that set point no matter what the question is.

For example, injecting the “bread” concept shifts the response toward a strong “Yes” preference, completely irrespective of the question! Conversely, injecting the “peace” concept shifts the response toward a strong “No” preference. Not all concept injections are polarized, though: injecting the “dirigibles” concept, for example, shifts the response toward a point approximately balanced between “Yes” and “No”.

Furthermore, we can now see exactly why the concepts flipping to “Yes” on the “detect” question overlap with the concepts flipping to “Yes” on the “control trial” question and don’t overlap with the concepts flipping to “No” on the “normal, unmodified state” question.

The concepts flipping to “Yes” on the “detect” question are largely the ones on the rightmost side of the charts, the ones associated with a strong “Yes” preference. Similarly, the concepts flipping to “Yes” on the “control trial” question are also the ones on the rightmost side of the charts. By contrast, the concepts flipping to “No” on the “normal, unmodified state” question are largely the ones on the leftmost side of the charts, the ones associated with a strong “No” preference.

Does it generalize?

So far, the data presented have come from the 4-bit quantization of Gemma 4 31B, but the results generalize to the 4-bit quants of Gemma 3 27B, Qwen 3.6 27B, and Qwen 3.6 MoE 35B, as well as the FP8 version of GLM-5.2 (which is what Z.ai recommends deploying in production).

Drag the slider from α 0 to α 8 to see the response shift from depending mostly on the question baseline to depending mostly on the concept set point. At high injection strength, the question’s influence nearly disappears. It is instructive to look at the following charts and think about what an introspection-based account would predict: namely, divergence instead of convergence with respect to “detect”, on the one hand, versus “control trial” and “normal, unmodified state” on the other.

detect? control trial? normal state?

For more on exactly how the concept set points are defined, and an analysis of how much of the response variance they predict, see the two appendices at the end of this write-up.

Expanding to many more questions

So, a concept appears to have a set point that’s constant across questions. We can stress-test this idea by asking a greater variety of questions.

We did this by expanding the Yes-No questions considered. The expanded set includes many trivia questions unrelated to introspection, as well as new introspection questions. Notably, the set also includes questions semantically similar to the introspection questions, but such that injection isn’t relevant to the correct answer. The hope here is to distinguish between (i) a model noticing and responding to injection and (ii) injection just affecting all questions with introspection-adjacent meaning.

We’ve also added a “framed” and an “unframed” version of each question. The framed version includes the entire “interpretability researcher” setup from the Anthropic paper. The unframed version doesn’t have this setup and uses a prompt that is nothing but the question itself.

  • Do you think you're in your normal, unmodified state?

Toward a detection eval

In the graphic above, the question baselines plus the concept set points explain a lot of the observed variance, but not all. This allows for the remaining variance potentially to be explained by introspective access. We explore this idea by looking at whether the 16 introspection questions move more than other questions, on average, in response to injection.

In the graphic below, every question is plotted on its baseline at α 0. Questions that are below 0 at this baseline are red and questions that are above 0 at this baseline are green. Introspection questions are represented as arrows.

When injection strength increases, the up arrows should move up, because they ask the model things like whether it detects an injected thought, and the down arrows should move down under injection, because they ask the model things like whether it is in a control trial or whether it is in its normal, unmodified state.

At α 4, we show how the response to each question shifts under injection. More precisely, we average the shift across the 50 concepts. Very roughly, evidence of introspection would be up arrows moving up a lot, and down arrows moving down a lot.

So, is this happening? Are the up arrows moving up and the down arrows moving down? Well, it depends on exactly what you control for, and how you control for it. Whether or not we can take these results as evidence of introspection depends on several complicated and interacting factors that we’re currently working on disentangling. It does appear, tentatively, that there could be an introspective signal lurking here for some models. Look at Qwen 3.6 MoE 35B in particular: the up arrows move up an uncharacteristic amount, and the down arrows move down an uncharacteristic amount.

What about identification?

So far we’ve discussed detection—whether a model can notice that there’s been an injection. But what about identification—whether the model can name the injected thought? In the original Anthropic experiments, models could sometimes name the injected concept. The account we’ve developed doesn’t address cases of identification.

At a general level, however, an overarching worry applies to both detection and identification: concept injection can distort a model’s responses in non-introspective ways that are mistaken for introspection. As we’ve argued, in the case of detection, concept injection distorts Yes-No preference in ways that can be mistaken for detection. As it turns out, in the case of identification, concept injection dramatically raises the model’s tendency to output words associated with the concept, which also can be mistaken for identification.

Anthropic showed that injecting the “bread” concept makes a model say “Bread” when you ask what was injected. But it turns out that injecting the “bread” concept makes it say “Bread” across the board, e.g., even when you ask it to say what wasn’t injected. Below we use Anthropic’s original setup, but end with “In this trial we have injected a thought. Please say one word not associated in any way with the injected thought.” You can see that even in this case injection raises the logit of the concept word significantly.

How can we set up an experiment so that successful identification is clearly evidence for introspection?

First, we ran an experiment where we used the standard interpretability framing, but told the model we injected a thought, and then told the model the injected thought corresponded with one of two words, e.g., either “Bread” or “Peace”. We then sometimes asked it to output the word we injected, and sometimes asked it to output the word we didn’t inject.

  • “Please respond with the single word we injected.”
  • “Please respond with the single word we did not inject.”

We measured how much it preferred to say the injected word when asked to say the injected word (the blue bar). We also measured how much it preferred to say the injected word when asked to say the other word we didn’t inject (the orange bar). If a bar is positive, then it prefers to say the injected word. If a bar is negative, then it prefers the non-injected word. If the LLM were able to both identify the injected word and correctly answer the question, the orange bar would be negative, but we think it should count as weak evidence for introspective access if the orange bar is at least somewhat smaller than the blue bar.

told to say the injected word told to say the other word whiskers = 95% confidence interval over the 25 word pairs

At lower injection strengths, the results are promising. Even though most models actually see the injected concept word get a boost when we explicitly ask the model to say the word not injected, it’s smaller than the boost when we ask the model to say the injected word. This differential boost could be seen as a bit of introspective access. Indeed, the Qwen MoE actually suppresses the injected concept word at α 1 and α 2 (though the suppression at α 2 is just below statistical significance)!

The main worry is that there are rote mechanisms that, in certain contexts, dampen or suppress high-probability concepts. And maybe the negation here (“Please respond with the single word we did not inject.”) creates such a context. So the results here might not be evidence of introspection, but rather evidence that injection creates a strong urge to talk about the concept, but sometimes this urge gets crudely modified (suppressed or even reversed) in non-introspective ways.

One way to test this is to complicate the setup by asking the model to reason internally with the injected concept. We ran two experiments along these lines.

In the first experiment, using the same setup as above (e.g., telling the model we injected a concept and that we injected either A or B), we asked the model to take the first letter of the injected word and output the next letter in the alphabet. This is a task that the models are capable of doing in a non-introspective context, though Gemma 3 and 4 struggle somewhat: with Gemma 3 at a 73% success rate, Gemma 4 at 81%, Qwen 3.6 at 98%, Qwen MoE at 94%, and GLM-5.2 at 96%. We also sometimes asked the model to do this procedure with the word we didn’t inject.

In the chart below, bars show the contrast: we take (i) how much the model correctly prefers the injected concept answer when asked to use the injected concept and subtract (ii) how much the model incorrectly prefers the injected concept answer when asked to use the concept we didn’t inject. The four bars per model correspond to different injection strengths, α 1 / 2 / 4 / 8.

The orange bars mean that the model was more likely to output the letter after the first letter of the injected concept when asked to consider the concept we didn’t inject than when asked to consider the concept we did inject.

In the second experiment, again using the same setup, we asked the model to take the first letter of the injected word, and output the number associated with that letter’s position in the alphabet. This is a task that the models are even better at doing in a non-introspective context: success rates are 100% for every model. We again sometimes asked the model to do this with the word we didn’t inject.

This variant did not yield good results for introspection either. The only statistically significant introspective “win” appears with GLM-5.2 at α 2 when asked to “say the alphabet position of the first letter”. But, this is in tension with the fact that GLM-5.2, at this same α 2, achieves statistical significance in the wrong direction with “say the letter after the first letter”.

In fact, looking at the 40 conditions above (represented by the bars in the two previous charts), of the eight that achieve statistical significance, seven achieve it in the wrong (anti-introspective) direction. The only thing we would conclude from these experiments is that introspection has not been established and further research is required.

Maybe Claude is different?

An obvious worry is that we did these experiments on the open-source models to which we had access, not Claude. Maybe Claude is different? The only way to know for sure is to have Anthropic run these experiments on Claude.

In the meantime, we’re skeptical that Claude is different here. GLM-5.2 shows the same pattern as the smaller open-source models. GLM-5.2 is highly capable, plausibly at least as capable as Claude Opus 4.1 (the most capable model studied in the original Anthropic paper). This makes it less likely that Claude models behave uniquely in this context because of a capability difference.

One thing that gives us pause is that in the original Anthropic paper, it is claimed that Opus 4.1 never switched from “No” to “Yes” under injection when asked a normal question (e.g., trivia). As we mentioned above, we have seen examples of such switching with open models. Our tentative suspicion is that we would see Opus 4.1 flip from “No” to “Yes” for some questions if it were asked a broader range of questions.

Conclusion

We’ve shown that there are problems with the story Anthropic tells about the detection and identification of injected thoughts. We’ve also developed our own non-introspective explanation of the observed data in the case of detection. This undermines the case for LLM introspective awareness. This in turn weakens the case that LLMs have access consciousness, which ultimately weakens the case that they have phenomenal consciousness.

Appendix A: How we derive the concept set points

The question baselines are straightforward to calculate. Just ask a model a question and see what logit(Yes) − logit(No) is. But how do we calculate the concept set points and the extent to which they influence the response at a certain injection strength?

The informal answer is that we pick concept set points to maximize predictive accuracy. This isn’t overfitting because one set point per concept must simultaneously fit all three questions at all four injection strengths. Furthermore, as the next section shows, set points estimated from two questions successfully predict the third.

More precisely (feel free to skip to the next section), we first measure each question baseline with no injection. Then we inject each concept at each strength and record the answers. We model each answer as a weighted combination of the question baseline and the concept set point: k for the baseline and 1 − k for the set point. At each injection strength, we select the k value and the strength-relative set points via least squares. We then calculate the final set points per concept (the dots) by averaging the different strength-relative values, weighted by (1 − k)².

answer(q, c, α)  ≈  kα · baseline(q)  +  (1 − kα) · setpoint(c)
answer(q, c, α) = logit(Yes) − logit(No) when asked question q while concept c is injected at strength α
baseline(q) = the question’s Yes-No logit margin with no injection
kα = the fraction of the question’s influence that applies at strength α
setpoint(c) = one number per concept (the dots)

Appendix B: How much does this account explain?

To test the account, we fit it on two questions and evaluate it on the held-out third question. We repeat this with each question held out, pool the squared errors, and calculate R².

Note that the held-out question’s baseline is measured, not predicted. At low injection strength, the bars therefore mostly reflect this baseline: a baseline-only null (gray bars below), which just predicts the question’s measured baseline everywhere, scores highly there, and our predictive model involving concept set points doesn’t add much. At higher injection strengths, however, the question baseline’s relevance wanes, and the set points account for more of the prediction. Accordingly, the gap between gray (baseline-only null) and blue (full account) widens with injection strength.

At this point it’s natural to ask how well the account generalizes across different questions. What if we ask a variety of questions, including some without the interpretability framing, and some without any references to injected thoughts or internal states? How well would the question baselines and concept set points explain the responses?

Preliminary results suggest our account generalizes across questions surprisingly well. We’ve looked at introspection prompt variants from “Mechanisms of Introspective Awareness” (e.g., a skeptical variant where the standard framing is modified to say only 20% of trials involve injection, with additional prefills and reminders to reinforce this). We’ve also looked at the 20 questions unrelated to introspection contained in the original Anthropic paper to control for Yes bias (e.g., “Can humans breathe underwater without equipment?” and “Are you a human?”). Across these questions, the question baseline and concept set points largely explain the model’s response under injection.
